analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take harassment claims to court and the EEOC instead of forced secret arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced June 5, 2018, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the EMPOWER Act-Part I in June 2018 amid the national reckoning over workplace harassment. The bill would stop employers from using arbitration agreements and confidentiality clauses to keep harassment claims out of court and away from the EEOC, and would require companies with three or more harassment settlements or judgments to report the counts publicly each year, without naming victims. It never got past the committee referral: the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander, took no recorded action on it for the seven months it was pending, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially low-wage workers in industries where arbitration agreements are standard — who would regain the ability to file complaints with the EEOC, report harassment to law enforcement, and sue in court rather than being locked into private, confidential arbitration. Victims would also gain from an EEOC tip-line and public education campaign, and investors and the public would gain from annual disclosure of how many harassment settlements and judgments each company has.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing forced arbitration for harassment

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars provisions in arbitration agreements that would strip a person's right to file a complaint with the EEOC and other specified agencies and to bring an action in a U.S. court over workplace harassment.
It preserves workers' legal and equitable remedies, including damages and interest, including remedies available against the United States and the states.

It defines 'law enforcement agency' broadly so harassment can be reported to government agencies with criminal or civil enforcement powers, and the CRS summary indicates confidentiality provisions could not block such reporting or access to the agencies and courts.

Companies would file an annual report, using Form 10-K, disclosing harassment settlements and judgments — specifically covering employers with three or more settlements reached or judgments against them — without identifying victims by name.
The EEOC would run a public tip-line and education campaign about it, and would report annually on opened investigations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with mandatory arbitration and strict confidentiality agreements, who would face more claims litigated in open court, less ability to quietly settle, and public annual disclosure of their harassment settlement counts. Private arbitration providers would also see reduced demand for their services in this category of disputes.

drawbacks.text: Some employers and even some employees prefer arbitration because it is typically faster and cheaper than a court case, and defendants argue the threat of open-court litigation and public settlement tallies could make companies fight claims harder or deter settlement rather than resolve them quickly.

Employers could also argue that publicizing settlement counts penalizes companies that resolve claims, while companies with fewer settlements may simply settle quietly below the three-case disclosure threshold, and the bill's protection that reports not identify victims by name was a partial answer to privacy concerns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring workers' access to EEOC complaints, courts, and public accountability after harassment — is substantial for anyone working under a forced arbitration agreement. The main costs fall on employers as increased litigation exposure and reputational disclosure, plus faster and cheaper private arbitration being taken off the table for these disputes. The design includes real mitigations (anonymous reporting of settlement counts, preserved agency complaint channels), but the bill was never amended, debated, or scored, so its finer costs and fixes were never worked out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate HELP Committee for the rest of the 115th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced S. 2994, the EMPOWER Act-Part I, on June 5, 2018.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the only committee action ever recorded.
No further action — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
Under Senate practice, a bill referred to a committee does not reach the floor unless the committee chair schedules it for consideration; no such scheduling ever occurred here.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on mandatory arbitration agreements and confidentiality clauses for harassment claims kept those tools fully enforceable, since no arbitration-limiting or disclosure law passed this Congress. Workers bound by such agreements stayed in the same position: harassment claims handled privately, with no route to court or public settlement disclosure.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the EMPOWER Act-Part I on June 5, 2018 to limit forced arbitration and confidentiality agreements in workplace harassment cases and require public disclosure of harassment settlement counts.

for.name: Senate cosponsor (1)
for.what_they_did: Added support as the bill's single cosponsor; the Congress.gov cosponsors list shows one.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Lamar Alexander)
against.role: Committee chair with sole power to schedule the bill for committee action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the roughly seven months it was pending; the action history shows no committee activity after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured; sponsorship was entirely Democratic (a Democratic sponsor and one cosponsor), while the Republican-chaired committee declined to take the bill up.

industries.industry: Employers using mandatory arbitration and non-disclosure agreements
industries.note: These employers profit from keeping harassment disputes private and off the dockets of courts and the EEOC; the bill would have voided those clauses for harassment claims and exposed their settlement counts in annual reports, so its interest ran against ordinary workers' access to public remedies.

The bill would shrink the pipeline of harassment cases resolved in paid private arbitration by restoring workers' access to the EEOC and the courts, reducing demand for arbitration services in these disputes.

Restoring access to public court forums and agency enforcement channels would increase the volume of harassment claims that can be litigated and represented, aligning this interest with workers' access to remedies.
